title: CBT — worry and sleep (session 4)

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Welcome back. Before we start, how has the week been, and what would you like us to make sure we cover today?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: It's been up and down. Work was really busy, and I didn't sleep well most nights. I'd like to talk about the sleep, I think.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Okay, so sleep is one item. Last week we agreed you'd try the worry diary. Shall we look at how that went as well, and then set the agenda from there?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yes. I did it four nights out of seven. I wrote the worries down but I'm not sure it helped much.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Four nights is a real effort, especially in a busy week. What did you notice when you looked back over what you'd written?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Most of them were about work. Like, what if I've missed something in the report and my manager thinks I can't cope.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: So a thought like 'I've missed something and my manager will think I can't cope'. When that thought shows up at night, how much do you believe it, from zero to a hundred?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: At night, probably eighty. In the morning it's more like thirty.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: That's a big difference between night and morning. What do you make of that?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I suppose at night everything feels worse. In the morning I can see it's probably fine.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: What happens next, after the thought comes at night? What do you do?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I check my emails on my phone. Sometimes for an hour. Then I'm wide awake.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: So the checking is meant to settle the worry, but it seems to keep you awake. Does that fit with the cycle we drew a few weeks ago?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Yes, it's the same loop. Thought, check, more awake, more thoughts.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: What evidence do you have, from the last month, about whether you actually miss things in your reports?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Honestly, nothing major. My manager said the last one was good. One small typo once.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: So one small typo, and positive feedback on the last report. If a friend had that record and was lying awake checking, what would you say to them?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: I'd tell them they're doing fine and the emails can wait until morning.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: How does it feel to say that?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: A bit strange. True, though.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: For this week, would you be willing to try an experiment? Phone charging in the kitchen, and if the thought comes, you write it in the diary and rate how much you believe it, then rate it again in the morning.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: The phone in the kitchen is going to be hard. But I can try it on work nights.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Work nights is a good start. What might get in the way?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: If I get an email from my manager late in the evening I'll want to answer it.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: What could you do in that moment instead?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Maybe write down what I'd reply and send it in the morning.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: That sounds workable. Before we finish, can I check how today's session was for you, and anything that wasn't helpful?

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: It was helpful. The friend question made me think. I'd like to keep working on the night-time thing.

segments.speaker: therapist
segments.text: Let me summarise: the worry diary showed most worries are about work, belief drops from eighty at night to thirty in the morning, and checking keeps you awake. This week, phone in the kitchen on work nights, diary and ratings. We'll review it next time.

segments.speaker: client
segments.text: Sounds good. Thank you.

expected_note_facts: Belief in worry ~80/100 at night vs ~30 in morning
Checks emails on phone at night, which keeps client awake
Recent positive feedback from manager; one minor typo
Homework: phone charging in kitchen on work nights; worry diary with belief ratings night and morning

strengths: Collaborative agenda setting that included homework review
Belief ratings used to make the night/morning difference visible
Linked the checking behaviour to the shared formulation (the cycle)
missed_openings: The fear of being seen as 'not coping' could have been explored as a possible underlying belief
Client said the diary 'didn't help much' — that disappointment wasn't explored
try_next: Explore the meaning of 'can't cope' with a downward-arrow question
